{{Short description|Mathematical construct}}
In mathematics, given an additive subgroup <math>\Gamma \subset \R</math>, the '''Novikov ring''' <math>\operatorname{Nov}(\Gamma)</math> of <math>\Gamma</math> is the subring of <math>\Z[\![\Gamma]\!]</math><ref>Here, <math>\Z[\![\Gamma]\!]</math> is the ring consisting of the formal sums <math>\sum_{\gamma \in \Gamma} n_\gamma t^\gamma</math>, <math>n_\gamma</math> integers and ''t'' a formal variable, such that the multiplication is an extension of a multiplication in the integral [[group ring]] <math>\Z[\Gamma]</math>.</ref><!-- what do you can call it? --> consisting of [[formal sum]]s <math>\sum n_{\gamma_i} t^{\gamma_i}</math> such that <math>\gamma_1 > \gamma_2 > \cdots</math> and <math>\gamma_i \to -\infty</math>. The notion was introduced by [[Sergei Novikov (mathematician)| Sergei Novikov]] in the papers that initiated the generalization of [[Morse theory]] using a closed one-form instead of a function. The notion is used in [[quantum cohomology]], among the others.

The Novikov ring <math>\operatorname{Nov}(\Gamma)</math> is a [[principal ideal domain]]. Let ''S'' be the subset of <math>\Z[\Gamma]</math> consisting of those with leading term 1. Since the elements of ''S'' are unit elements of <math>\operatorname{Nov}(\Gamma)</math>, the [[Localization (commutative algebra)|localization]] <math>\operatorname{Nov}(\Gamma)[S^{-1}]</math> of <math>\operatorname{Nov}(\Gamma)</math> with respect to ''S'' is a subring of <math>\operatorname{Nov}(\Gamma)</math> called the "rational part" of <math>\operatorname{Nov}(\Gamma)</math>; it is also a [[principal ideal domain]].

== Novikov numbers ==
Given a [[Smoothness|smooth function]] ''f'' on a [[Differentiable manifold|smooth manifold]] <math>M</math> with nondegenerate critical points, the usual [[Morse theory]] constructs a free [[chain complex]] <math>C_*(f)</math> such that the (integral) rank of <math>C_p</math> is the number of critical points of ''f'' of index ''p'' (called the Morse number). It computes the (integral) [[Homology (mathematics)|homology]] of <math>M</math> (cf. [[Morse homology]]): 
:<math>H^*(C_*(f)) \cong H^*(M,\Z)</math> 

In an analogy with this, one can define "Novikov numbers". Let ''X'' be a connected polyhedron with a base point. Each cohomology class <math>\xi \in H^1(X,\R)</math> may be viewed as a linear functional on the first homology group <math>H_1(X,\R)</math>; when composed with the [[Hurewicz homomorphism]], it can be viewed as a group homomorphism <math>\xi\colon \pi=\pi_1(X) \to \R</math>. By the universal property, this map in turns gives a [[ring homomorphism]], 
:<math>\phi_\xi\colon \Z[\pi] \to \operatorname{Nov} = \operatorname{Nov}(\R)</math>, 
making <math>\operatorname{Nov}</math> a module over <math>\Z[\pi]</math>. Since ''X'' is a [[Connected space|connected]] polyhedron, a [[local coefficient system]] over it corresponds one-to-one to a <math>\Z[\pi]</math>-module. Let <math>L_\xi</math> be a local coefficient system corresponding to <math>\operatorname{Nov}</math> with module structure given by <math>\phi_\xi</math>. The homology group <math>H_p(X, L_\xi)</math> is a finitely generated module over <math>\operatorname{Nov},</math> which is, by the [[structure theorem for finitely generated modules over a principal ideal domain|structure theorem]], the direct sum of its free part and its torsion part. The rank of the free part is called the Novikov Betti number and is denoted by <math>b_p(\xi)</math>. The number of cyclic modules in the torsion part is denoted by <math>q_p(\xi)</math>. If <math>\xi = 0</math>, <math>L_\xi</math> is trivial and <math>b_p(0)</math> is the usual Betti number of ''X''.

The analog of [[Morse inequalities]] holds for Novikov numbers as well (cf. the reference for now.)
